The Nicobar pigeon Caloenas nicobarica is a large, robust columbid endemic to the small islands and coastal forests of Southeast Asia and the Indo-Pacific. Neonates emerge from the egg after an incubation period of approximately 28 days [ab = approximately 28 days], a duration recorded in captive colonies where eggs were maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. At hatching, the semi-precocial chick is covered in down but is entirely dependent on parental provisioning, and its wet weight at birth has been measured at 18.6 grams [Wwb = 18.6 grams], a modest initial mass that reflects the relatively small clutch size typical of this species. Adult body mass, representing the ultimate wet weight attained through growth, reaches a markedly higher value of 519 grams [Wwi = 519 grams], placing the Nicobar pigeon among the heavier members of the Columbidae family. This substantial increase from hatchling to adult size underscores a prolonged period of somatic development supported by intensive biparental care and a diet rich in fruits and seeds.

Under the elevated thermal conditions characteristic of fully active metabolic function in this tropical bird, which stabilizes near an internal temperature of 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C], the fledging period is completed relatively rapidly. Young birds achieve their first flight and leave the nest at approximately 37 days after hatching [tx = approximately 37 days after hatching], a milestone marking the transition from a sedentary, brooded nestling to a mobile, though still dependent, fledgling at a temperature of 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C]. This timing aligns with the developmental pace observed in other large, frugivorous island pigeons, where the need to escape terrestrial predation accelerates the achievement of flight capability. The nestling phase is characterized by rapid feather growth and a high metabolic demand, which the parents meet through frequent regurgitative feedings. The departure from the nest does not signify full independence, as the fledglings continue to receive parental food deliveries for several additional weeks while they refine their foraging skills and learn to navigate the forest canopy.

Sexual maturation in the Nicobar pigeon is attained at 111 days after hatching [tp = 111 days after hatching], again under the standard active body temperature of 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C]. This relatively early onset of puberty for a bird of this size suggests a life history strategy that balances the risks of delayed reproduction against the energetic costs of early gonadal development. In captive populations, the attainment of reproductive maturity is indicated by the onset of courtship behaviors and cloacal inspection, although first successful reproduction typically occurs somewhat later. The corresponding age at first brood, marking the production of the first viable clutch, is reached at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime. The interval between reaching sexual maturity at 111 days and producing the first viable clutch at 365 days represents a strategic reproductive delay, likely governed by the time needed for territory establishment and mate acquisition in the densely occupied island forests.

The Nicobar pigeon exhibits an exceptionally conservative reproductive output consistent with its low fecundity and extended lifespan. The species produces a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], a very small clutch size that is extreme even among columbids, which typically lay one to two eggs. Furthermore, females initiate only one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], yielding a maximum reproductive rate of one offspring per year [Ri = one offspring per year]. This very low annual reproductive potential, when considered against the risks of predation and environmental stochasticity on small islands, necessitates a high rate of adult survival to maintain population stability. The thermal conditions under which this slow-paced reproduction occurs are the same as those governing other life-history events, measured at 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C]. The combination of a single-egg clutch and a single annual nesting attempt likely reflects strong energetic constraints imposed by the high cost of provisioning a rapidly growing, semi-altricial chick with a protein-rich crop milk diet.

Maximum longevity in the Nicobar pigeon is considerable, with the oldest documented individuals reaching an age of 20.5 years [am = 20.5 years], a value recorded under a standard operating body temperature of 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C]. This extended lifespan, approaching two decades, is unusually long for a bird of this mass and is more typical of long-lived seabirds and large parrots. The profound disparity between the low annual reproductive output of a single egg and this long lifespan points to a life history strategy heavily reliant on adult persistence rather than high fecundity to offset mortality. Field observations suggest that adult survival rates are exceptionally high, with individuals showing strong site fidelity to their nesting islands. This evolutionary trajectory is consistent with the low predation pressure and stable resource availability characteristic of isolated island ecosystems, where the risk of reproductive failure can be amortized over many breeding seasons, allowing even a single chick per year to sustain the population over time.
